1.s: John the Baptizer prepares the way, Jesus is baptized and tested in the wilderness, then calls fishermen to follow him and heals many people in Galilee.
1.d: Mark’s Gospel is about Jesus, the good news [[tosn:Mark 1:1]]. It opens with John the Baptist in the wilderness, the “voice” Isaiah foretold, preparing people for Jesus’ message of God’s kingdom [[tosn:Mark 1:3]] [[tosn:Mark 1:4]] [[bsn:Mark 1:1-20]]: “The time is fulfilled, and God’s Kingdom is at hand!” [[bible:Mark 1:15]]

2.s: Jesus forgives and heals a paralysed man let down through a roof, calls the tax collector Levi, eats with sinners, and claims authority over the Sabbath.
2.d: Five conflict stories are grouped together (2:1–3:6), each showing Jesus’ great authority [[tosn:Mark 2:1-3:6]]. Only God can forgive sins, yet Jesus forgives them, and his hearers understood this as a claim to God’s own authority [[tosn:Mark 2:5]] [[tosn:Mark 2:6-7]].

3.s: Jesus heals on the Sabbath, angering the Pharisees, chooses twelve apostles, and answers the charge that he drives out demons by Satan’s power. His family comes to take him home.
3.d: The story of Jesus’ family wraps around the argument about driving out demons, linking two groups who misunderstand him [[tosn:Mark 3:20-35]]. His true family are those who do God’s will [[bible:Mark 3:35]].

4.s: Jesus teaches in parables: the sower, the lamp, the growing seed and the mustard seed. Then he calms a storm on the lake, and the disciples ask, “Who is this?”
4.d: Jesus’ parables, with Isaiah 6:9–10, show that those who refuse to believe will not understand [[tosn:Mark 4:11-12]]. Calming the storm shows him stronger than every danger around his disciples [[bsn:Mark 4:35-5:20]].

5.s: Jesus frees a man possessed by a “Legion” of demons, heals a woman who touches his cloak, and raises the daughter of Jairus, a synagogue leader.
5.d: Mark sets the healing of the bleeding woman inside the story of Jairus’s daughter [[tosn:Mark 5:21-43]]. Her illness had also made her ceremonially unclean [[tosn:Mark 5:24-34]]. “Talitha cumi” is Jesus’ own Aramaic, the language he spoke [[tosn:Mark 5:41]].

6.s: Jesus is rejected in Nazareth, sends out the Twelve, and feeds five thousand people with five loaves and two fish. Herod has John the Baptizer beheaded, and Jesus walks on the water.
6.d: Calling Jesus “the son of Mary” rather than of Joseph likely means Joseph had died [[tosn:Mark 6:3-4]]. Seeing the crowd “like sheep without a shepherd”, Jesus shepherds and feeds them [[tosn:Mark 6:34]] [[bsn:Mark 6:30-44]].

7.s: Jesus challenges traditions about washing, teaching that evil comes from within, then heals the daughter of a Greek woman and a deaf man.
7.d: Mark explains Jewish washing customs for his non-Jewish readers [[tosn:Mark 7:2-4]]. What makes a person unclean comes from the heart, not from food [[tosn:Mark 7:14-23]]; Mark adds that Jesus was “making all foods clean” [[bible:Mark 7:19]].

8.s: Jesus feeds four thousand, heals a blind man in two stages, and Peter declares, “You are the Christ.” Jesus then foretells his death and resurrection and calls followers to take up their cross.
8.d: Peter’s confession that Jesus is the Christ, and Jesus’ first warning of his death, are the turning point of Mark [[tosn:Mark 8:27-38]]. Only Mark tells of the healing in two stages, which may picture the disciples’ slowly opening eyes [[tosn:Mark 8:22-26]].

9.s: On a high mountain Jesus is transfigured before Peter, James and John. He heals a boy whose father cries, “I believe; help my unbelief,” and teaches that the greatest must be the servant of all.
9.d: Moses and Elijah may show the law and the prophets fulfilled in Jesus [[tosn:Mark 9:4]]. The voice corrects Peter: Jesus is the beloved Son, not their equal, and the disciples must listen to him [[tosn:Mark 9:7]].

10.s: Jesus teaches about divorce, blesses children, and tells a rich man to sell everything and follow him. He says he came “to give his life as a ransom for many”, and heals blind Bartimaeus.
10.d: “The Son of Man also came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” [[bible:Mark 10:45]]; “many” likely echoes Isaiah 53:12 [[tosn:Mark 10:45]]. Bartimaeus, who follows Jesus at once, is an example for all who come to him [[bsn:Mark 10:46-52]].

11.s: Jesus rides into Jerusalem on a colt to shouts of “Hosanna!”, curses a fig tree, and drives traders from the temple, calling it a house of prayer.
11.d: The withered fig tree is a prophetic sign act, like those of the earlier prophets [[tosn:Mark 11:13-14]], and wraps around the temple scene as a sign of judgement on Israel’s failure to follow God [[bsn:Mark 11:12-26]].

12.s: Jesus tells the parable of the wicked tenants and answers trick questions about taxes, the resurrection and the greatest commandment. He praises a poor widow’s gift.
12.d: The greatest commandment joins the Shema, “Listen” (Deuteronomy 6:4–5), with love for one’s neighbour [[tosn:Mark 12:29-31]]. On taxes, Jesus neither backs the rebels nor simply supports Rome: loyalty to God comes first [[tosn:Mark 12:17]].

13.s: Jesus foretells the destruction of the temple and speaks of wars, persecution and the coming of the Son of Man, urging his followers to watch.
13.d: Jesus speaks on the Mount of Olives about the temple’s destruction. Scholars differ on how much points to the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70 and how much to the coming of the Son of Man at the end of the age [[tosn:Mark 13:5-23]] [[tosn:Mark 13:24-27]].

14.s: A woman anoints Jesus, Judas agrees to betray him, and Jesus shares the Passover meal, giving bread and wine as his body and blood. He prays in Gethsemane, is arrested, tried before the high priest, and Peter denies him three times.
14.d: The Last Supper is linked with the Passover meal [[tosn:Mark 14:12-32]], and the cup is the blood of the covenant, poured out for many [[tosn:Mark 14:24]]. In the garden Jesus prays “Abba, Father”, showing his closeness to God [[tosn:Mark 14:35-36]] [[bible:Mark 14:36]]. At his trial he speaks of the Son of Man at God’s right hand, as in Psalm 110:1 [[tosn:Mark 12:36]] [[bible:Mark 14:62]].

15.s: Pilate hands Jesus over to be crucified. He is mocked, nailed to a cross, cries out “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” and dies. The temple curtain tears, and a centurion confesses him as the Son of God.
15.d: Jesus cries out the words of Psalm 22:1 in Aramaic, the language he spoke [[tosn:Mark 15:34]]. The one mocked as king really was the King, serving his people by giving his life [[bsn:Mark 15:16-39]], and a Gentile officer declares, “Truly this man was the Son of God!” [[tosn:Mark 15:39]] [[bible:Mark 15:39]]

16.s: On Sunday morning women find the tomb empty and a young man tells them Jesus has risen and will meet his disciples in Galilee. They flee in fear. Later verses tell of appearances and the great commission.
16.d: Two of the oldest and best Greek manuscripts end at 16:8, with the women afraid. Nearly all scholars think verses 9–20 were written by someone other than Mark, and many doubt Mark meant to stop at 16:8 [[tosn:Mark 16:9-20]]. The translators of the World English Bible keep them as reliable [[webfn:Mark 16:9]].
